title: Calls for justice from family of woman shot dead by Calgary police officer
article: Family members of an Indigenous woman shot and killed by a Calgary police officer are demanding justice for their slain cousin.
Robin Fiddler, 34, was rushed to hospital where she later died after being shot twice by a Calgary police officer early Wednesday morning.

"We believe Robin didn't deserve to die - we want to see justice," said the victim's cousin, Mario Fiddler. "We believe the Calgary police officer could've taken different steps dealing with Robin (and that) a Taser could've been used instead of shooting our cousin. My cousin isn't the type of person to be an aggressor."

Calgary police responded to the 2000 block of 35th Street S.E. around 6:30 a.m. for reports of a suspicious person, which first started coming in half an hour earlier. The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) said Robin pepper-sprayed the unidentified female officer who was still sitting in her patrol car after arriving at the scene.

When the officer got out of her car to arrest Robin, a struggle ensued that resulted in the woman being fatally shot. The pepper spray container was later found wrapped in black tape with the label and the description of the container's contents obscured.
Calgary police Chief Mark Neufeld said Friday the officer was wearing a police-issued, body-worn camera at the time of the shooting.
Robin, from the Waterhen Lake First Nation in northern Saskatchewan, had been moving back and forth between Saskatchewan and Calgary, her family said.
"She was in the trades, doing construction. She was always in good spirits and she loved the city of Calgary," Mario said.
Robin's other cousin, Angela Fiddler, said she was never a woman to let tough times get her down.

"She always tried to get through whatever systemic barriers that she faced - she always tried to make a way," she said, adding she had taken Robin under her wing. "She was just a blessing to us. It was her smile, she was always so funny and she always wanted to make people laugh.

"When we were both younger, I just took her under my wing and that was that. She would come live with me when she had the opportunity. I've always had an open door for her. Robin was a beautiful soul, she deserved to live."
Mario said their family is in the process of returning Robin's body to Saskatchewan so the family can lay her to rest and begin a traditional healing journey.
Robin's death marks the third fatal incident involving Calgary police this year, all of which are being investigated by ASIRT.

In May, an unidentified man went into medical distress and died after police - responding to what they called a "targeted" hit-and-run - used their Tasers following a struggle. Earlier this month, a woman, also unidentified, fell to her death from a fifth-storey balcony in Chinatown as police executed a search warrant. Police said there was no physical contact with the woman before she went over the balcony.
